slides.title: Chorus Ledger
items: A listening service for wetland restoration
Illustrative seed pitch

slides.title: Who heard the pond last night?
items: Restoration teams visit a site a few times each season. Calling can start between visits. A quiet survey sheet leaves the project ecologist with little evidence about the intervening nights.
Chorus Ledger rents listening stations and returns a season of recordings with clips a biologist can check.

slides.title: Leave a listener at the waterline
items: The station records short windows after dusk. A field technician swaps the card on a planned visit and checks the microphone against a reference tone.
The lab proposes candidate calls. A reviewer listens to each retained clip, attaches a confidence note and returns uncertain calls for follow-up.

Dark marks indicate a confirmed call. Pale marks indicate a reviewed recording with no confirmed call. Read clockwise from the top, one mark per night.

slides.title: From raw audio to an evening’s review
items: Review hours per station-week • modeled workflow
8 → 2 hours
For the same sample week, the reviewer spends two hours checking flagged clips and a random sample of quiet intervals. The pilot measures missed calls against a fully reviewed subset.

slides.title: A season, priced per station
items: For a twelve-week season, the customer receives a loaned recorder, candidate clips, human review and a signed evidence file.
$720 direct cost
The example assigns $320 to review, $220 to equipment wear and $180 to logistics. That leaves $1,080 per station-season before overhead.

slides.title: The first buyer already writes the report
items: We sell to ecology consultancies that prepare annual monitoring reports for restoration clients. One approved subcontract can serve several sites under the same project lead.
The evidence file includes dates, station locations, reviewed clips and an explicit list of recording gaps.

slides.title: A focused first territory
items: 30 practices
Four projects per practice, three station-seasons per project. At $1,800 each, full adoption would yield $648,000 in annual sales.
How we qualify a project
The buyer has site permission, a named reviewer and a reporting deadline within the season. We decline work where the recording plan cannot answer the client’s question.

slides.title: What the pilot must prove
items: Coverage
At least 90% of scheduled recording windows should yield usable audio. Reviewers log wind, flooding and equipment faults separately.
Agreement
A second ecologist reviews a blind sample. Species-level disagreements stay visible in the evidence file until adjudicated.
Renewal
The project lead signs off on the exported record and requests a priced deployment for the following season.

slides.title: Two people sign the record
items: Nell Hart · field ecology
Nell designs the sampling plan with the project ecologist. She owns permits, station placement and the list of conditions that make a night unusable.
Idris Vale · acoustic systems
Idris owns recorder uptime, detection software and clip provenance. The first hire is a reviewer who can reproduce a decision from the archived recording.

slides.title: One season to earn the next
items: Before dusk
Sign four paid pilots. Check the field plan and reference recording with each buyer.
During the season
Deploy 24 stations and audit a sample weekly. Replace failing hardware on the next field visit.
At handover
Deliver the evidence files and price renewals. Expand only after two buyers commit to another season.

slides.title: Back the first full chorus
items: $900k seed
$390k for field hardware and operations, $310k for acoustic review tools and $200k for customer pilots. The round funds a 15-month plan.
The test at month 15
Twenty-four deployed stations, four paid pilots and two renewal commitments. All venture details and figures are illustrative.
